Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

more adverb

to a greater degree: more beautiful, love more

also more … than, -er (bigger, faster), rather than, love more, more suitable, more necessary, know better, he thinks he knows better, know best, think one knows better

classical

Cic. Fam. 14.3.5: mihi tē cārius nihil esse
Lewis & Short s.v. comparātīvus: gradus, the comparative (Donatus)

gradus comparātīvus

the comparative degree of an adjective or adverb (cārior, citius), with quam or the ablative of the thing compared

the comparative: dearer, more beautiful, faster

Latin says “more” with the ending: cārior, dearer; citius, faster. “Than” is quam, or the ablative of what is compared: plūs oculīs meīs (Catull. 14.1). “Much more” is multō with the comparative, “a little more” paulō (see a lot, a little).

Other words

  • magis — more, rather

    adverb · also used · classical · Sen. Ep. 78.22: magis juvat bibere sitientem; Publil. Sent. N 35: Nīl magis amat cupiditās, quam quod nōn licet.

    With verbs, and with adjectives that make no comparative, most of them with a vowel before the ending (idōneus, necessārius): magis idōneus, better suited; magis … quam, more than, rather than (Vulg. Act. 20.35).

  • plūs — more (with verbs: love more, be worth more)

    adverb · also used · classical · Catull. 14.1: nī tē plūs oculīs meīs amārem; Cic. Q. fr. 3.1.7: plūs ut illum amēs quam ipse amō

    “Love more” is plūs amāre. For “more” of a thing, see more. Classical prose does not put plūs with an adjective: “more suitable” is magis idōneus.

Examples

  • nī tē plūs oculīs meīs amārem

    if I didn’t love you more than my own eyesCatull. 14.1

  • nōn enim concēdō tibi plūs ut illum amēs quam ipse amō

    for I don’t grant that you love him more than I doCic. Q. fr. 3.1.7

  • magis juvat bibere sitientem, grātior est ēsurientī cibus

    drink gives more pleasure to the thirsty, and food is more welcome to the hungrySen. Ep. 78.22

  • Nīl magis amat cupiditās, quam quod nōn licet.

    Desire loves nothing more than what is not allowed.Publil. Sent. N 35

  • cūrā ut valeās et ita tibi persuādeās, mihi tē cārius nihil esse nec umquam fuisse

    look after your health, and be sure that nothing is or ever was dearer to me than youCic. Fam. 14.3.5

  • Beātius est magis dare, quam accipere.

    It is more blessed to give than to receive.Vulg. Act. 20.35

  • tempus hoc magis idōneum quam umquam anteā

    this time, better suited than ever beforeCic. Fam. 1.2.3

  • nūllum enim officium referendā grātiā magis necessārium est

    for no duty is more necessary than returning a kindnessCic. Off. 1.47

  • Tibi, pater, permittimus: plūs scīs quid factō opus est.

    We leave it to you, father: you know better what needs doing.Ter. Ad. 995–996

  • quem quī audiunt intellegere etiam et sapere plūs quam cēterōs arbitrantur

    those who hear him think he understands and knows more than the restCic. Off. 2.48 (Lewis & Short, s.v. sapiō)

  • Cēnset sē plūs sapere quam mē.

    He thinks he knows better than I do.Traupman 102

See also more, most, less, a lot, the more …, the more …, rather.
